/-!
# Erdős Problem 379

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/379](https://www.erdosproblems.com/379)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos379

open Filter

noncomputable def S (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup {s | ∀ k ∈ Finset.Ico 1 n, ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ p^s ∣n.choose k}

/--
Let $S(n)$ denote the largest integer such that, for all $1 ≤ k < n$, the binomial coefficient
$\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by $p^S(n)$ for some prime $p$ (depending on $k$).Then
$\limsup S(n) = \infty$.

This was formalized in Lean by Tao.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,

theorem erdos_379 : atTop.limsup (fun n => (S n : ℕ∞)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

end Erdos379

reformulations.difference: Lean totalizes the source's maximum over all natural n, assigning S 0 = S 1 = 0. At these two inputs the admissibility condition is vacuous, so the natural-number sSup takes its default value rather than representing a maximum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≥ 2 the admissible exponents form a nonempty bounded set: exponent 0 is admissible, and the k = 1 condition gives a prime p with p^s ∣ n, hence s < p^s ≤ n. Thus sSup is exactly the largest admissible exponent. The only theorem uses the limsup at infinity, which is unchanged by the values at 0 and 1. In scratch.lean I proved the maximum characterization, both boundary values, invariance under changes below 2, and the equivalence of the theorem's proposition with ∀ r N, ∃ n ≥ max 2 N, ∀ k, 1 ≤ k → k < n → ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ p^r ∣ n.choose k.
